passage:
Dear Deepika,

I joined the water-rights march on Sunday, and I want to tell you how it felt. We gathered at the park gate and walked together to the town hall, chanting a line the organisers gave us. It was surprising how quiet I felt inside. My legs were shaky at first, but the calm of the crowd carried me. Before we started, I noted the two exits, kept my phone charged, and stayed near the marshals with bright bands. When the crowd got tight near the main road, I stepped to the side. I'm glad I went. It felt good to say something with my body, not just my posts. Come next time, if you want.

Trisha

qa.q: Where did the marchers gather?
qa.a: They gathered at the park gate.

qa.q: What did Trisha feel during the march, and what helped Trisha?
qa.a: Trisha felt quiet inside after being shaky at first, and the calm of the crowd carried Trisha along.

qa.q: What safety steps did Trisha take that a wise person might copy?
qa.a: Trisha noted the exits, kept the phone charged, stayed near the marshals and stepped aside when the crowd got tight.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel reading Trisha's invitation?
qa.a: Deepika may feel curious and a little cautious, since Trisha describes both the calm and the precautions Trisha took. 🙂

grounding: Trisha joins a peaceful march to voice a concern and stays aware of safety and exits.

passage: I'm Sharmila, and last month I stood in a line of students outside the district office holding a placard about the college bus routes. I'd never done anything like this. Our chant was simple, and our teacher, Minakshi, had told us to keep it peaceful and to check with the police about where we could stand. My heart was thumping. I looked at the girl next to me, and she squeezed my arm. Before we began I found the gate we'd use to leave if it got crowded. Nothing bad happened. An officer took our letter and said it would go up. I don't know whether it will change anything, but I felt heard for the first time.

qa.q: What was written on Sharmila's placard about?
qa.a: The placard was about the college bus routes.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling at the start, and what might have steadied Sharmila?
qa.a: Sharmila felt nervous, with her heart thumping, and the friendly squeeze from the girl beside her and knowing the exit likely steadied Sharmila.

qa.q: What preparations helped keep the protest safe?
qa.a: They kept it peaceful, checked with the police about where to stand, and Sharmila found the gate to leave if it became crowded.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt about the students marching?
qa.a: Minakshi probably felt responsible and proud, given that she gave them safety advice and encouraged peaceful conduct.

grounding: Sharmila joins a peaceful student protest, voicing concern while keeping to rules and knowing the way out.

passage: I'm Chinmay, and I went with Bhavna to the march for better street lighting outside our campus after two students were mugged near the bus stop. She had painted a sign: "LIGHT THE ROAD." At the gathering point, before the march began, I saw her check the route map the organisers had shared and point out the side lane near the temple. "If it gets messy, we go there," she said. We walked slowly, chanting "Safe roads, bright roads!" Bhavna's voice was clear and steady. Near the main gate, a group of men from outside the college began shouting and pushing. Bhavna's face tightened. She didn't shout back. She tapped my arm, and we moved to the side lane with three others. From there we watched the organisers talk to the police, and the march continued peacefully. Later, she posted photos of the sign, not the fight.

qa.q: What did Bhavna's sign say?
qa.a: "LIGHT THE ROAD."

qa.q: What might Bhavna have been feeling when the men began shouting and pushing?
qa.a: Her tightened face suggests she felt worried and tense, but she stayed calm and determined, choosing to move away rather than shout back.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do to stay safe while protesting?
qa.a: She checked the route and an exit lane before the march, and moved to it with others when the pushing started.

qa.q: How did Chinmay see Bhavna during the march?
qa.a: Chinmay saw her as clear and steady, chanting calmly and making sensible choices when things turned tense.

grounding: Shows through an observer a young adult expressing a concern through peaceful protest while staying aware of safety and exit routes.

passage:
Monday. The ward's water supply in Aurangabad had failed for three weeks. Shankar and his friend Devika decided to join the residents' march to the municipal office on Thursday. That evening Shankar read the permission letter the residents' committee had got from the police and noted the route.
Thursday. Two hundred people walked with empty pots, chanting "Paani do!" Shankar held one end of the banner; Devika held the other. When the road narrowed near the bridge and the crowd bunched, Shankar remembered the side street the committee had marked. He guided a group of older women that way. Devika kept the chant going.
Saturday. The municipal commissioner met a committee of five, and a tanker came to the ward that evening. Shankar was proud, but tired. "I didn't know shouting slogans could feel so calm," he said. Devika laughed. "Because we had a plan."

qa.q: What did the marchers carry?
qa.a: Empty pots.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling after the march?
qa.a: He felt proud of what they achieved, but also tired from the effort.

qa.q: What preparations made the march safer?
qa.a: Reading the police permission letter, knowing the route and a side street to use when the crowd bunched.

qa.q: How did Devika see the calm feeling during the march?
qa.a: Devika thought it came from having a plan in advance.

grounding: Shows a young adult expressing a concern through a peaceful march while staying aware of rules and exit routes.

passage: Hafsa, you're asking if you should go to the march on Saturday. Let your Rehana Khala tell you about mine. I was twenty, a college student in Hyderabad, when a girl from our hostel was attacked on her way home. We were so angry. Thirty of us made candles and posters and walked from the college to the police station, silent, just holding the candles. Silence felt stronger than shouting. Before we left, our warden, a strict woman, made us write her number on our wrists and told us the lanes to use if anything went wrong. Halfway there, some boys on bikes started jeering. I felt my heart pound, but we did what she'd said: stayed together and didn't answer. At the police station, the inspector came out and met us. Go, beti. Just go with friends, know your way out, and remember your voice matters most when it's calm.

qa.q: What did the warden make the students write on their wrists?
qa.a: Her number.

qa.q: How did young Rehana feel when the boys on bikes started jeering?
qa.a: She was frightened, her heart pounding, but stayed calm and kept to the plan with the others.

qa.q: What choice inside the story kept the march safe and peaceful?
qa.a: The students stayed together and didn't answer the jeering, following the warden's instructions about lanes and her number.

qa.q: How did the warden treat the march?
qa.a: She supported it but planned for safety, giving them her number and exit lanes before they left.

grounding: Shows a young adult expressing concern through a peaceful silent march while staying aware of safety and exits.

passage: The climate march through Guwahati began at the college gate at ten, and by noon the heat was brutal. Lakshmi walked near the front with a cardboard sign, "Save our wetlands," chanting with the others until her throat was raw. Before starting, she and Bhupen had agreed on two things: stay near the volunteers in green caps, and if they got separated, meet at the bookshop on the corner of the lane behind the stadium. Near the district office the police had set up barricades. Most marchers stopped, sang and sat down on the road as planned. But a handful at the back started shoving and shouting at the officers. The crowd tightened. Lakshmi looked round; Bhupen was gone. Her heart thumped. She stepped sideways out of the press, followed a green cap to the lane behind the stadium, and texted him. Ten minutes later he appeared at the bookshop with two bottles of water. "Did the pushing start near you?" he asked. "Yes. So I left."

qa.q: Where had they agreed to meet if they got separated?
qa.a: At the bookshop on the corner of the lane behind the stadium.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when the crowd tightened and Bhupen was gone?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt anxious and frightened, heart thumping, yet stayed calm enough to follow their plan.

qa.q: Which safety steps helped Lakshmi during the march?
qa.a: Agreeing a meeting point in advance, staying near the volunteers, and stepping out of the crowd as soon as the pushing started.

qa.q: How might the officers at the barricade have seen the march?
qa.a: Mostly as a peaceful sit-in with singing, with tension coming only from the few who shoved.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult voicing a cause through a peaceful march with chants and signs, while staying aware of safety and exit routes.
